key_insight: A compressible finite-chord model can predict leading-edge noise reduction from perforated and porous inserts without fitted constants by deriving the insert admittance from geometry and flow physics.
engineering_relevance: This gives aeroacoustic designers a more transferable way to screen leading-edge treatments for wind-turbine, aircraft, and duct applications using measurable material properties instead of test-calibrated impedances.
method: Solve the finite-chord scattering problem in compressible subsonic flow with wake shedding, Kutta condition, and permeability-dependent edge singularities.

Represent perforates via Rayleigh conductivity plus corrections for plate thickness, aperture interaction, and grazing-flow blockage; represent porous inserts using measured permeability and pore-fluid inertia.
Include finite-span and array-aperture effects in the far field and compare predictions against measurements.
evidence_signal: For three perforated inserts across four flow conditions, the model matches measurements to 2.5 dB rms over 84 comparisons, improving on 4.4 dB rms for the previously scaled-impedance approach; two porous inserts are predicted within 1.7 dB rms.
watch_item: The model does not explain narrow equally spaced spectral peaks seen on perforated plates, suggesting an additional convecting source mechanism not captured by the frozen-gust formulation.
paper_title: Leading-edge noise reduction by perforated and porous inserts: a compressible finite-chord prediction without fitted constants
